title: Understanding Global Dimming

pages.text: Global dimming is a reduction in sunlight reaching the Earth. It is caused by air pollution, especially sulfate aerosols. This decrease in solar energy was noticed when measurements started in the 1950s. Industrial pollution increased air particles, leading to less visible sunlight over the following decades.
pages.caption: Hotspots of sulfate aerosol pollution in 2005–2007 are highlighted in orange. Such sulfates rarely occur naturally outside of volcanic activity, and their increased levels are the main cause of global dimming.

pages.text: The sunlight dropped by four to five percent every ten years until the 1980s. Air pollution increased during these years because of post-war industrial growth. Solar activity did not change much during this period.
pages.caption: Satellite snapshot of atmospheric sulfur dioxide on 15 April 2017. Sulfur dioxide forms highly reflective sulfates, which are considered the main cause of global dimming.

pages.text: Aerosols have a cooling effect on the atmosphere. Global dimming has hidden the true extent of global warming. In the 1970s, heavily polluted regions even experienced cooling while the rest of the world warmed.
pages.caption: Early 2010s estimates of past and future anthropogenic global sulfur dioxide emissions, including the Representative Concentration Pathways. While no climate change scenario may reach Maximum Feasible Reductions (MFRs), all assume steep declines from today's levels. By 2019, sulfate emission reductions were confirmed to proceed at a very fast rate.

pages.text: Since the 1980s, cleaner air has led to a partial reversal of global dimming. This is sometimes called global brightening. This brightening has helped speed up global warming since the 1990s.

Global dimming refers to a measured reduction in sunlight reaching the Earth's surface. First noticed when systematic solar measurements began in the 1950s, this phenomenon is driven by atmospheric particulate matter, predominantly sulfate aerosols originating from industrial air pollution.
pages.caption: Hotspots of sulfate aerosol pollution in 2005–2007 are highlighted in orange. Such sulfates rarely occur naturally outside of volcanic activity, and their increased levels are the main cause of global dimming.

evidence.articleCaption: Hotspots of sulfate aerosol pollution in 2005–2007 are highlighted in orange. Such sulfates rarely occur naturally outside of volcanic activity, and their increased levels are the main cause of global dimming.

pages.text: Between the 1950s and the 1980s, visible sunlight weakened at a rate of four to five percent per decade. This decline coincided with rising air pollution from post-war industrialization, while solar activity remained relatively stable.

Global dimming is characterized by a sustained reduction in surface solar irradiance driven by atmospheric particulate matter. Predominantly composed of sulfate aerosols from anthropogenic air pollution, this attenuation of sunlight was documented shortly after systematic measurement programs commenced in the 1950s.
pages.caption: Hotspots of sulfate aerosol pollution in 2005–2007 are highlighted in orange. Such sulfates rarely occur naturally outside of volcanic activity, and their increased levels are the main cause of global dimming.
